title: Did Your Eyes Deceive You, or Did You See at Wasit
intro: Al-Sukkari introduces this ode as al-Akhtal's praise of his own people and satire on Jarir. A glimpse of al-Rabab at daybreak sets off a series of doubts about love before the speaker appeals to what she knows of his clan's hospitality. The horses of Taghlib carry the account of tribal encounters, first in their scarred bodies and then in the traces they leave elsewhere. The closing attack puts Jarir's father on a balance against the great men of Darim.

translation: Did your eyes deceive you, or did you see at Wasit,
in the last dark of night, a vision of al-Rabab?
1.sharh: He questions the instrument of recognition, his own eye. Al-Mubarrad also allows the opening to be an assertion of error, followed by a second thought as the vision persists.

translation: She crossed your path at al-Abalikh after
breaking off affection and all contact at Abraq.
2.sharh: The two place names hold two different moments. The woman ended the relationship in one place, and her image can still intercept him somewhere else.

translation: A woman of the jinn changed shape to startle us.
Beautiful women show you terrors.
3.sharh: The vision's power to appear in another shape makes it uncanny. He treats the lover's unsettling experience of beauty as something akin to meeting a spirit.

translation: From their passing fancies they stretch towards young desire
a long cord with which to catch the wayward.
4.sharh: What begins as a passing inclination extends far enough to become a snare. The adjective “long” is held until the end, stretching the cord through the line.

translation: I have never seen cunning like theirs when it works
among us, or cords to match their snares.
5.sharh: The cord from the preceding verse multiplies into snares. His claim is one of experience, since he says he has seen the tricks operating among his own companions.

translation: They give insults as presents to those they love
and gracious words to those they cannot bear.
6.sharh: A gift usually declares goodwill, yet the gift here is abuse. Polite speech is no safer guide, since it is reserved for the unwanted suitor.

translation: They keep faith as long as they see you there.
Once you grow restless, they too turn away.
7.sharh: Presence sustains the pact. When he tires of it they grow restless in turn, and a word from the same root passes from one side of the relationship to the other.

translation: Whenever they promise you a favour, they fail to give it.
At the end of their promises you find delay.
8.sharh: A lover becomes like a creditor left waiting past the due date. The language of a promised favour slips into that of a debt persistently deferred.

translation: If they call you their uncle, that kinship
only worsens your standing with them.
9.sharh: “Uncle” sounds affectionate. To a suitor it can also mean he has been assigned an older, securely unromantic place in a woman's life.

translation: If you weigh their judgement against youthful longing,
longing outweighs their judgement and tips the pan.
10.sharh: The ear almost sees the scales move as desire comes down and judgement rises. A second set of scales near the end will test the claims of Jarir's family.

translation: Is this a final breach, Umm Mukhallad,
or coyness? This coyness has lasted long.
11.sharh: He at last addresses one woman directly. Her long reserve has come to look exactly like dismissal, and his repetition of the word for coyness leaves the distinction unresolved.

translation: You know, when the pregnant camels come home
with an ostrich chick's short steps, felled by a north wind
12.sharh: Pregnant camels, ordinarily valuable and protected, stumble home like young ostriches. The storm prepares a demanding test of the household's hospitality.

translation: that pelts the thorn trees with icy missiles
till snow lies in heaps upon the branches,
13.sharh: Snow strikes the trees like small stones and stays piled on them overnight. The weather still interrupts the syntax of “you know”, delaying the answer until the need is unmistakable.

translation: that we hurry fresh meat to our guest
before our household, and that we strike down champions.
14.sharh: The promise implicit in “you know” is finally met. In the winter shortage a guest receives freshly slaughtered meat ahead of the family, and the boast then turns from feeding to fighting.

translation: Sons of Kulayb, mine are the two uncles who
killed kings and struck off shackles.
15.sharh: Kulayb is Jarir's clan. Calling the two Taghlib champions his uncles brings a tribal past within the intimate language of family.

translation: Their brother al-Saffah kept his horses thirsty
till they reached the water of al-Kulab, parched.
16.sharh: A third forebear brings his horses to the disputed water with a thirst deliberately unrelieved. The approach to al-Kulab turns that thirst into part of the battle story.

translation: Out from the pass at al-Kulab they come against them,
at the trot of beasts racing for scant water.
17.sharh: The horses now become the active subject for a long stretch of verse. Predators hurrying towards a trickle of water make their short racing strides visible.

translation: Each led horse is powerfully built,
easy on the rein, seeming to strut.
18.sharh: Al-Sukkari understands a horse led on the march and ridden when the fight begins. Its strength and its easy response to the rein meet in a gait that looks almost like a strut.

translation: And a firmly made mare bears weapon marks on her chest,
as if red dye lay across her breast.
19.sharh: The red stain looks as though someone dyed the mare's breast. Its position tells us she faced the source of the wounds.

translation: Their bellies tucked, they have drawn lean from night travel
and from pursuit when battle meets them.
20.sharh: Their outline records two sorts of exertion, long night journeys and the quick changes of pursuit. A shape admired in a horse here bears witness to what it has undergone.

translation: Pale with salt across their backs, they seem dressed
in coverings of water when the sweat dries.
21.sharh: Evaporation leaves the white salt behind. A horse's ordinary covering is a cloth, while these horses wear a covering deposited by their own exertion.

translation: Seldom at morning are they anything but gaunt,
meeting whatever turn the times bring.
22.sharh: There is seldom a morning of recovery between encounters. The horses seem to ride into fortune's changes on their own account, taking on the part of their riders.

translation: With their breast they ground down the kings' company
until blood made sandals for their feet.
23.sharh: Abu Amr al-Shaybani glosses the royal “company” as an assembled body. The picture runs from the horses' crushing breast to their hooves, shod in the casualties' blood.

translation: They destroyed your people, Jarir, and others,
and destroyed whole encampments of al-Ribab.
24.sharh: The rider's taunt reaches its living addressee. Named camps and an alliance enlarge the claim beyond the losses of Jarir's immediate people.

translation: They entered Shaqiq's very house
and saw the mole upon Nadra's leg.
25.sharh: A private bodily mark stands for the loss of a household's privacy. It is a taunt about what the invaders could see, offered in the impossible form of testimony from their horses.

translation: And the sons of Ghudana, eyes staring,
run on foot beneath their bellies.
26.sharh: The men's fixed eyes and their position below the mounts tell the story. The last word explicitly puts them on foot, far below the prestige of the mounted warrior.

translation: They carried them off as dogs carry their pups,
till they reached Ura'ir and Uthal.
27.sharh: The image strips the captives of a say in their destination. The two watering places give a geographical end to the forced journey.

translation: They looked sidelong at Riyah after
making spear-shade over Dabba.
28.sharh: Spears massed overhead have cast what looks like shade on Dabba. The sidelong look towards Riyah threatens to carry that same, hostile shelter elsewhere.

translation: They left no girl just grown among al-Ghawadir
without snapping the anklet on her leg.
29.sharh: The broken anklet substitutes one small, visible injury for the larger ordeal of a raided settlement. The speaker extends it, by a sweeping boast, to every girl coming of age.

translation: Al-Hudhayl rose against you and reached you
at Irab, where he portions out the spoils,
30.sharh: The general and the water of Irab identify another encounter. Dividing the plunder is shown as an accomplished fact and stands in for the preceding defeat.

translation: with a host crying the Araqim's name, whose
horsemen were neither unarmed nor helpless in the saddle.
31.sharh: The war cry identifies a group within Taghlib. Its riders have both arms and horsemanship, so neither lack of equipment nor an insecure seat diminishes the force.

translation: On horses drawn about the face, as though
the labour of galloping had given them wasting sickness.
32.sharh: The horses look like sufferers from a wasting illness. The simile measures the physical cost of repeated galloping in animals previously distinguished by their strength.

translation: They wheeled on Fazara in a charge,
like the returning gaming arrow, and ranged there at will.
33.sharh: The manih was returned to the bundle for successive draws in the old game of lots. The comparison catches the cavalry coming back into play, then moving freely across the ground.

translation: They gave their foes a bitter cup to drink
and brought down the fortune of al-Hubab's house.
34.sharh: Defeat is a drink that must be swallowed. A family's good fortune then goes from being something the horses dislodge to something that has departed altogether.

translation: They pass over Kahil's corpse, stripped bare,
and Ibn al-Muhazzam, whom they have left abased.
35.sharh: Two names replace the collective enemy. Returning to a stripped corpse makes humiliation outlast the fighting, as does the final term for the second man's condition.

translation: They killed those who bore arms and others besides,
and left you their routed remnant to feed.
36.sharh: He includes people who carried no weapon in this boast about killing. The survivors become Jarir's dependants, a cruel inversion of the hospitality claimed for the speaker's own house.

translation: Al-Jahhaf wept for what they had done
at al-Shar'abiyya when he saw the children.
37.sharh: Al-Jahhaf's tears give the boast a witness from the other side. Al-Sukkari says that seeing the children brought home to him the deaths of their fathers.

translation: Jarir, you took on a task beyond your strength
and showed your mother's nakedness to fools.
38.sharh: Jarir's decision to enter the exchange is itself put on trial. Al-Akhtal presents the exposure of his mother to public abuse as something the son's own challenge has brought about.

translation: When both branches of Wa'il rise towards glory
and the whole valley gathers and floods against you,
39.sharh: Bakr and Taghlib share the ancestor Wa'il. Their combined force is a watershed emptying into one channel, and the unfinished sentence leaves Jarir immediately below it.

translation: you are a speck on a wave of muddy foam,
flung by the oncoming flood and lost for good.
40.sharh: The flood does not even have to struggle with its opponent. As a mote on the surface he is moved wherever the current throws him and then disappears.

translation: They trod the sacred stations at Mina
until they cast mountains upon mountains.
41.sharh: Horses mass above the hills until they too look like mountains. Al-Sukkari links the boast to Kulayb's leadership at Khazaz, while the pilgrimage stations at Mina give the verse its visible landscape.

translation: Go call to your sheep, Jarir. All
your wishes promised you in private was delusion.
42.sharh: The herdsman's call deliberately cuts across the noise of armies. His private sense of importance, the speaker insists, gives him no public rank amongst these people.

translation: You told yourself you could stand level with Darim
or balance against Hajib and Iqal.
43.sharh: Darim is the clan of al-Farazdaq, Jarir's rival. Two named men give the idea of family standing tangible weights for the scales introduced by the verb.

translation: Put your father in the balance with theirs
and its iron jumps towards you, his side flies up.
44.sharh: The scale tips violently because the father's side is light. Prestigious ancestry has become something an onlooker could read off a piece of iron without a word of testimony.

translation: Authority and strength in numbers belong to Darim.
Their brother makes light of heavy burdens,
45.sharh: Abu Ubayda understands the paired nouns as leadership and numerous followers. One member's willingness to shoulder a heavy collective obligation stands for the group's capacity.

translation: those who hold the water till they drink
its first clear draughts, and divide it by the bucket,
46.sharh: Their claim to precedence is visible at a water source. They drink the best of it first and then apportion the supply in large bucketfuls.

translation: while the Wallow's son holds back his donkeys,
driven off like a stray she-camel, tasting no moisture.
47.sharh: Jarir cannot secure even a drink for his donkeys. His mother's insulting nickname evokes a place where animals roll, and his animals share the fate of a stranger's camel driven away from the herd.

1.1.5.head: واسِط
1.1.5.meaning: Wasit, a place by the Euphrates in al-Akhtal's poetry where he sees the apparition.

1.2.1.head: غَلَس
1.2.1.meaning: The darkness that still lingers as dawn approaches.

1.2.4.head: الرَّباب
1.2.4.meaning: Al-Rabab, the woman seen in his dream. A different name in verse 24 denotes a tribal alliance.

2.1.3.head: الأَبالِخ
2.1.3.meaning: Al-Abalikh, the place of the renewed encounter in the love prelude.

2.2.2.head: أَبرَق
2.2.2.meaning: Abraq, where the speaker recalls their relationship breaking off.

3.1.1.head: تَغَوَّلَ
3.1.1.meaning: Changed shape like a ghoul in traditional accounts.

3.2.1.head: غانِيَة
3.2.1.meaning: Beautiful women, traditionally glossed as those whose looks suffice without adornment.

4.2.1.head: سَبَب
4.2.1.meaning: A cord, here the line of a snare.

5.2.3.head: حِبال
5.2.3.meaning: Their snares, figured as a hunter's cords.

7.2.5.head: مِذال
7.2.5.meaning: Inconstant or easily wearied, here plural.

8.2.4.head: مِطال
8.2.4.meaning: Putting someone off, as in delaying payment of a debt.

9.2.4.head: خَبال
9.2.4.meaning: Ruin or impairment, here of his prospects as a lover.

11.1.2.head: الصَّريمَة
11.1.2.meaning: A decisive break in a relationship.

11.1.4-5.head: أُمّ مُخَلَّد
11.1.4-5.meaning: Umm Mukhallad, the name in the recited verse and its caption. Al-Sukkari gives Umm Muhallim, as does the video's separate glossary.

12.1.4.head: عُشَراء
12.1.4.meaning: She-camels some ten months gone in pregnancy and especially valuable.

12.2.1-2.head: هَدَج الرِّئال
12.2.1-2.meaning: “The short steps of ostrich chicks”, a rapid, unsteady gait.

13.1.3.head: حاصِب
13.1.3.meaning: A blast hurling stony pellets, here of ice or snow.

14.1.3.head: العَبيط
14.1.3.meaning: Fresh meat from an animal slaughtered in sound condition for a guest.

15.1.1-2.head: بَنو كُلَيب
15.1.1-2.meaning: Banu Kulayb, Jarir's clan within Tamim.

15.1.4.head: عَمّ
15.1.4.meaning: Two men of Taghlib whom he calls his uncles. Al-Sukkari names Abu Hanash and Dawkas. Other accounts identify the pair differently.

16.1.2.head: السَّفّاح
16.1.2.meaning: Al-Saffah, a Taghlib leader associated with the battle of al-Kulab. Accounts differ over his personal name.

16.2.3.meaning: Water drawn and collected at a watering place.

16.2.4.head: الكُلاب
16.2.4.meaning: Al-Kulab, a water source commemorated in accounts of tribal fighting.

16.2.5.head: نِهال
16.2.5.meaning: Thirsty and coming up for the first drink.

17.2.4.head: الأَوشال
17.2.4.meaning: Trickles or scant pools of water.

18.1.3.head: مُجتَنِب
18.1.3.meaning: A horse led on the march and kept fresh to ride in battle, in al-Sukkari's gloss. Nasir al-Din understands a spirited horse that is hard to mount.

18.1.5.head: أَسر
18.1.5.meaning: The strength and compactness of its build.

18.2.1-2.head: سَلِس القِياد
18.2.1-2.meaning: “Easy on the rein”, responsive to guidance.

19.1.1.head: مُمَرَّة
19.1.1.meaning: A firmly built mare, with the suggestion of a tightly twisted rope.

19.2.4.head: جِريال
19.2.4.meaning: A red dye used as a comparison for blood.

20.1.1-2.head: قُبّ البُطون
20.1.1-2.meaning: “Tucked at the belly”, lean through the flanks.

21.1.1-2.head: مُلح المُتون
21.1.1-2.meaning: Pale along the back with dried salt.

21.2.5.head: جُلّ
21.2.5.meaning: Protective cloths or coverings for mounts.

22.2.2-4.head: مِن عُرَض الحَوادِث
22.2.2-4.meaning: From whatever events happen to present themselves.

23.1.2-3.head: حائِرَة المُلوك
23.1.2-3.meaning: “The kings' company”, their assembled body in Abu Amr al-Shaybani's gloss. Qabawa takes it as their picked men.

23.1.4.head: كَلكَل
23.1.4.meaning: With the breast, the part that bears down when an animal kneels.

23.2.2.head: اِحتَذى
23.2.2.meaning: Put on shoes, here the blood coating the horses' hooves.

24.2.4.head: الرِّباب
24.2.4.meaning: Al-Ribab, a tribal confederation. Its first vowel differs from that of the woman in the opening verse.

24.2.5.head: حِلال
24.2.5.meaning: Groups camped together in their own settlements.

25.1.4.head: شَقيق
25.1.4.meaning: Shaqiq, identified in the diwan's notes with Banu Dabba.

25.2.4.head: نَضرَة
25.2.4.meaning: Nadra, Shaqiq's wife in the commentary. The mole on her leg is invoked to claim access to a private space.

26.1.1-2.head: بَنو غُدانَة
26.1.1-2.meaning: Banu Ghudana, a branch of Yarbu of Tamim.

26.2.4.head: راجِل
26.2.4.meaning: On foot, as distinct from the mounted men.

27.2.3-4.head: عُراعِر وَأُثال
27.2.3-4.meaning: Ura'ir and Uthal, two watering places marking the journey's end.

28.1.4.head: رِياح
28.1.4.meaning: Riyah, a division of Yarbu associated with Jarir's people.

28.2.2.head: ضَبَّة
28.2.2.meaning: Dabba, a tribe associated with the Ribab confederation.

29.1.5.head: الغَواضِر
29.1.5.meaning: Al-Ghawadir, Banu Ghadira. Qabawa identifies them here with Asad. Nasir al-Din identifies them with Qays.

30.1.4.head: الهُذَيل
30.1.4.meaning: Al-Hudhayl ibn Hubayra, a Taghlib commander in the account of Irab.

30.2.1.head: إِراب
30.2.1.meaning: Irab, a watering place of Riyah that gave its name to an encounter.

31.1.4.head: الأَراقِم
31.1.4.meaning: Al-Araqim, the collective name of several divisions of Taghlib.

31.2.4.head: كِفل
31.2.4.meaning: Poor horsemen unable to hold a seat, also glossed as cowards.

32.1.2-3.head: ساهِمَة الوُجوه
32.1.2-3.meaning: Drawn and discoloured in the face through exertion.

33.1.4.head: فَزارَة
33.1.4.meaning: Fazara, a tribe of Ghatafan against whom the cavalry turns.

33.2.1-2.head: كَرّ المَنيح
33.2.1-2.meaning: “The return of the manih”, a lot repeatedly put back into the bundle for another draw.

34.2.3-4.head: بَنو الحُباب
34.2.3-4.meaning: The house of al-Hubab, associated with Umayr ibn al-Hubab of Sulaym.

35.1.3.head: كاهِل
35.1.3.meaning: Kahil, one of the dead named in the taunt, identified with Qays in the diwan's notes.

35.2.1-2.head: اِبن المُهَزَّم
35.2.1-2.meaning: Ibn al-Muhazzam, the second man named in the account of the dead.

36.2.2.head: فَلّ
36.2.2.meaning: The routed remnants of a force.

37.1.3.head: الجَحّاف
37.1.3.meaning: Al-Jahhaf ibn Hakim al-Sulami, an opponent of Taghlib in its fighting with Qays.

37.2.1.head: الشَّرعَبِيَّة
37.2.1.meaning: Al-Shar'abiyya, the site of an encounter between Taghlib and Qays.

38.1.2.head: جَشِمَ
38.1.2.meaning: Undertook a difficult or burdensome task.

39.1.4-5.head: فَرعا وائِل
39.1.4-5.meaning: “The two branches of Wa'il”, Bakr and Taghlib, regarded as brothers in tribal genealogy.

40.1.2.meaning: A floating mote or speck of debris.

40.2.2.head: الأَتِيّ
40.2.2.meaning: An incoming flood sweeping down from elsewhere.

41.1.4.head: المَشاعِر
41.1.4.meaning: The stations associated with the rites of pilgrimage.

41.1.6.head: مِنى
41.1.6.meaning: Mina, one of the pilgrimage sites near Mecca.

43.1.5.head: دارِم
43.1.5.meaning: Darim, al-Farazdaq's branch of Tamim, set above Jarir's clan in this challenge.

43.2.4-5.head: حاجِب وَعِقال
43.2.4-5.meaning: Hajib ibn Zurara and Iqal ibn Muhammad ibn Sufyan, leading men of Darim in the diwan's notes.

44.2.2.head: حَديدَة الميزان
44.2.2.meaning: The iron indicator on a balance, which moves as the pans tip.

44.2.4.head: شالَ
44.2.4.meaning: Rose up, as does the lighter side of a balance.

45.1.2.head: العَرارَة
45.1.2.meaning: Authority or precedence in Abu Ubayda's gloss, also explained as valour.

45.1.3.head: النُّبوح
45.1.3.meaning: Numerous followers, the assembled strength of a people.

46.2.1.head: عَفوَة
46.2.1.meaning: The first, clear draughts from the water supply.

46.2.3.head: سَجل
46.2.3.meaning: Full bucketfuls used to apportion water.

47.1.1-2.head: اِبن المَراغَة
47.1.1-2.meaning: “The Wallow's son”, a lampooner's name for Jarir through an insult to his mother.

47.1.4.head: عَير
47.1.4.meaning: His asses, plural of the word for an ass.

47.2.1-2.head: قَذف الغَريبَة
47.2.1-2.meaning: “Driving off the stranger”, as a she-camel from another herd is kept away from water.

47.2.5.head: بِلال
47.2.5.meaning: Enough moisture even to wet the throat.
